lead: An exhaust bench does not measure “pollution” as one number. It measures each gas by a physical effect that belongs to that gas: CO and CO₂ absorb infrared light, NO gives off light when it meets ozone, hydrocarbons make ions in a hydrogen flame, and smoke blocks light or blackens paper. Every engine change and every certificate is proved on such a bench, so its readings, and its mistakes, decide what a controller or an examiner believes.
prereq: You need: the gases and particles of formation of CO, HC and NOx and smoke and particulate matter.

blocks.text: Many wrong emission numbers are sampling errors, not analyser errors. For engine-out work the probe sits before the first catalyst; for a tailpipe test, after the last device. The line to the bench is heated to about 190 °C so water and heavy hydrocarbons stay as vapour, and a filter keeps soot out of the gas analysers. If the line runs cold, water condenses, dissolves NO<sub>2</sub> and takes heavy HC with it, and the reading falls.

Each analyser wants its sample in a different state. The flame ionisation detector takes the hot, wet gas. The infrared and chemiluminescence analysers take gas that has passed a cooler or water trap, because water absorbs infrared and quenches the chemiluminescence light. The smoke meter takes raw, unfiltered exhaust, because soot is what it measures.

On a steady test bed the bench samples raw exhaust. For a vehicle on a driving cycle, constant-volume sampling (CVS) dilutes the whole exhaust with filtered air to a fixed total flow and fills bags with a proportional sample, which the bench reads after the test.

sections.h3: NDIR for CO and CO₂, and oxygen by magnetism

blocks.text: NDIR means non-dispersive infrared: a broad infrared source is used without a prism or grating. A chopper sends the beam alternately through a sample cell and a reference cell filled with a non-absorbing gas. The detector is itself filled with the gas to be measured (CO, for a CO analyser), so it responds only to the wavelengths that gas absorbs; that is how the analyser picks its gas without dispersing the light. CO absorbs near 4.7 µm and CO2 near 4.3 µm.

blocks.where: I₀ and I are the light entering and leaving the cell; a is the absorption coefficient of the gas; c its concentration; L the cell length (the Beer–Lambert law). The analyser is calibrated with a zero gas (nitrogen) and a span gas of known concentration.

blocks.text: NDIR suits CO and CO2, whose bands are strong. It is poor for low-ppm NO and for hydrocarbons, whose absorption is weak and overlaps water. Oxygen does not absorb in the infrared; it is measured by its magnetism. O2 is paramagnetic (attracted into a magnetic field), and a paramagnetic analyser measures that pull.

The chemiluminescence detector (CLD) mixes the sample with ozone made inside the instrument: NO + O3 → NO2* + O2. The star marks an excited molecule; as it drops back it gives off light, which a photomultiplier counts. The light is proportional to NO. NO2 does not give this light, so for total NOx the sample first passes a heated converter that turns NO2 into NO.

items: Bypass the converter: the reading is NO.
Send the sample through the converter: the reading is NOx (apparent).
True NO<sub>2</sub> = apparent NO<sub>2</sub> ÷ η, where η is the converter efficiency (0 to 1).

blocks.text: The converter efficiency is checked by feeding it a gas of known NO<sub>2</sub> content and dividing the NO<sub>2</sub> it converts by the NO<sub>2</sub> offered. Water and CO<sub>2</sub> quench the excited molecules, so the sample is dried or the reading corrected.

sections.h3: FID for hydrocarbons, and smoke meters

blocks.text: The flame ionisation detector (FID) burns the sample in a small hydrogen flame. Organic carbon atoms form ions, and an electrode collects them. The current depends on the number of carbon atoms, not of molecules, so the reading is in ppmC: ppmC = ppm of the compound × its number of carbon atoms. One ppm of propane, C3H8, reads about 3 ppmC. The FID is blind to CO, CO2 and water, and gives low readings for oxygenated compounds such as methanol and formaldehyde. A heated FID at about 190 °C keeps heavy HC from condensing; a non-methane cutter burns every hydrocarbon except methane, so total HC minus the cutter reading gives non-methane HC.

Smoke is measured with light. An opacimeter (the Hartridge type is the classic) shines light across a fixed path of exhaust and reports opacity in per cent or the absorption coefficient k in m⁻¹. A filter-paper meter draws a fixed volume through white paper and reads its blackness as a Bosch smoke number from 0 to 10, or a filter smoke number. Neither gives PM mass; that needs a gravimetric filter weighed on a microbalance.

examples.question: A chemiluminescence analyser reads 380 ppm with the NO<sub>2</sub> converter bypassed and 420 ppm with the converter in line. The converter efficiency is 0.92. Find the true NO<sub>2</sub>, the true NOx and how much the uncorrected bench under-reports.
steps: Converter in line: apparent NOx = 420 ppm.
Under-report = 423.5 − 420 = 3.5 ppm, about 0.8 % of the reading.
examples.answer: True NO<sub>2</sub> is 43.5 ppm and true NOx 423.5 ppm; the uncorrected bench reads 3.5 ppm low.

examples.question: An NDIR CO analyser transmits 70 % of the light (I/I₀ = 0.70) with a 2.0 % CO span gas and 80 % with the engine sample. Assuming Beer–Lambert behaviour, find the CO in the sample.
steps: From I/I₀ = e<sup>−acL</sup>, ln(I/I₀) is proportional to c.
A straight-line guess from the transmissions, 2.0 × (1 − 0.80)/(1 − 0.70) = 1.33 %, would be 6 % high: the response is not linear.
examples.answer: The sample holds 1.25 % CO. Real analysers store a curve made from several span gases for the same reason.

traps: Comparing an FID reading in ppmC directly with a limit for one compound: divide by the carbon number first (90 ppmC of propane is 30 ppm).
Forgetting the converter efficiency: the apparent NO<sub>2</sub> is always low and must be divided by η before adding it to NO.
Letting the sample line run cold: water condenses, takes NO<sub>2</sub> and heavy HC, and the bench reads low.
Treating opacity or a Bosch number as PM mass: they measure light extinction or blackness; mass needs a filter and a balance.
Using NDIR for low-ppm NOx or HC: its absorption is weak and overlaps water; use the CLD and the FID.

quiz.q: What does NDIR stand for, and which two exhaust gases does it measure?
Write the reaction a chemiluminescence analyser uses.
quiz.a: NO + O<sub>3</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub>* + O<sub>2</sub>; the excited NO<sub>2</sub>* gives off light as it relaxes.

quiz.q: Why does an FID report ppmC rather than ppm?
quiz.a: Its ion current depends on the number of carbon atoms that reach the flame, so a molecule with three carbons gives about three times the signal of one with a single carbon.

quiz.q: Why does the smoke meter take raw exhaust while the gas analysers take filtered gas?
quiz.a: The filter protects the gas analysers from soot, but soot is exactly what the smoke meter must see; a smoke meter after the filter would read almost clean gas.

quiz.q: An FID reads 90 ppmC on a propane sample. What is the propane concentration?
A CLD reads 250 ppm bypassed and 275 ppm in line; η = 0.90. Find the true NOx.
quiz.a: Apparent NO<sub>2</sub> = 25 ppm; true NO<sub>2</sub> = 25 ÷ 0.90 = 27.8 ppm; true NOx = 250 + 27.8 = 277.8 ppm.

quiz.q: The NOx reading drops when the sample line is allowed to cool below the dew point. Explain the cause and the direction of the error.
quiz.a: Water condenses in the line and dissolves NO<sub>2</sub> before it reaches the converter, and remaining vapour quenches the light; both make the reported NOx too low.

beyond: Not for the exam. Portable emission measurement systems (PEMS) put compact analysers and a flow meter on a vehicle so emissions are checked on real roads. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) benches measure many gases, including ammonia and N<sub>2</sub>O, from one spectrum; laser absorption sensors reach low ppm in milliseconds. Particle counters with a condensation nucleus counter now support particle-number limits. Search next for “PEMS”, “FTIR exhaust analysis” and “condensation particle counter”.

figure.caption: The bench of the worked example. The smoke meter takes raw exhaust because soot is what it measures; the FID takes the hot, wet sample; NDIR and the oxygen cell take dried gas. The CLD reads 380 ppm with its converter bypassed and 420 ppm through it, and the converter efficiency of 0.92 turns the 40 ppm difference into 43.5 ppm of NO₂.

spec.aria: Exhaust bench: a probe feeds a raw smoke meter and a heated line at 190 degrees with a soot filter. The heated line feeds a heated FID for hydrocarbons and a cooler; the dry sample feeds NDIR for CO and CO2, a paramagnetic oxygen cell and a chemiluminescence detector whose converter has efficiency 0.92, reading 380 parts per million bypassed and 420 in line, so true NOx is 423.5.
